title: Lattice QCD Confirms the Strong CP Problem Is Real
hook: The strong force is allowed to violate CP symmetry, but the neutron refuses to show it. A lattice calculation pins how unnaturally small that knob must be: one part in 100 billion.
key_points: QCD permits a CP-violating term whose size is set by a free parameter, the theta angle.
A non-zero theta would give the neutron a measurable electric dipole moment; experiments see none.
The puzzle is why nature picked a value so close to zero — the strong CP problem.
The team computed the neutron's dipole moment sensitivity to theta directly from lattice QCD.
They used the Feynman-Hellmann theorem with a background electric field and domain wall fermions.
Comparing to experiment gives a bound on theta of roughly 1e-11, confirming the fine-tuning is real.
content_html: Quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force, contains a term that would violate CP symmetry. Its strength is set by a free parameter, the theta angle, and nothing in the theory says how big it should be — a number of order one would be perfectly natural. Yet if theta were anywhere near one, the neutron would carry a sizeable electric dipole moment, and decades of ever more sensitive experiments have failed to find one. That mismatch is the strong CP problem, and it is a leading motivation for the axion.
extra_html:
Turning the experimental non-detection into a bound on theta requires knowing how strongly the neutron's dipole moment responds to it, and that is a non-perturbative QCD calculation — the coupling is too strong for the usual expansion, so the theory has to be simulated on a discretised spacetime lattice.

Thomas Blum and colleagues report a new route to it. Rather than the usual approach, they apply the Feynman-Hellmann theorem, computing the dipole moment from the matrix element of the local topological charge density between nucleon ground states that a background electric field has spatially polarised. Those states have mixed spatial parity and are constructed through variational analysis. Working with 2+1 dynamical domain wall fermions at pion masses of 340, 420 and 576 MeV and a lattice spacing near 0.11 fm, they extract a statistically significant signal and extrapolate to the physical point.

The result implies the theta angle must be smaller than roughly 10^-11 — confirming, as the authors put it, that the strong CP problem genuinely exists rather than being an artefact of an imprecise calculation. They note the same local-topological-charge method should extend to other CP-violating interactions.

related.title: Measuring the force that traps a quark inside the proton
related.hook: Nobody has ever seen a free quark. A sharpened reconstruction of the actual force tugging on one inside the proton comes out looking like a string pulled at constant tension.

related.title: Hunting Solar Axions With Ancient Lead
related.hook: A detector built from archaeological lead was designed to catch supernova neutrinos. It turns out the same crystals are a competitive net for axions streaming out of the Sun.

related.title: Is the Muon Lopsided? Still No Sign of It
related.hook: A particle with a permanent electric dipole moment would violate time-reversal symmetry and point straight at new physics. Muon g-2 just squeezed the muon's limit tighter — and it stays at zero.

related.title: The Standard Model
related.hook: Almost everything around you is built from a handful of particles obeying three forces — and one theory predicts it all with jaw-dropping precision, yet still can't explain gravity.

flashcards.prompt: What is the strong CP problem?

choices.text: QCD allows a CP-violating term, but nature's value for it is unnaturally close to zero
The strong force violates CP symmetry far more than experiments can explain
CP violation has never been observed in any interaction

flashcards.explanation_html: The theta angle could be anything of order one, yet the absent neutron electric dipole moment forces it below about 1e-11 — a suspicious fine-tuning.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the neutron's electric dipole moment the key measurement here?
flashcards.back_html: A non-zero theta angle would give the neutron a dipole moment proportional to it, so the experimental non-detection translates into a bound on theta.

flashcards.prompt: Why is this calculation hard enough to need a lattice?
flashcards.back_html: The effect lives in non-perturbative QCD, where the coupling is too strong for perturbation theory — so the theory is simulated on a spacetime lattice instead.
